S07.asr: Her check grew, but prices grew more, so today it buys less than her first check did. If her first check bought 10 crates of everything the index tracks, her check today buys about 9.

S24.asr: Ruth isn't the worst case. And she isn't the best. Carl, also illustrative, took the same kind of rising check in January 1966. His 20 years had the fastest price rise of any stretch, 6 .38 % a year. Like Ruth's, his first check bought a row of 10 crates. On every one of his 20 anniversaries, his check bought less than it had the year before. Ruth's check climbed back Back in her early years, Carl's never did.

S27.asr: Edna, also illustrative, started in January 1949, the last starting month, when a two percent raise kept up. Twenty years later, her check still bought at least what her first one did. She is part of that early handful, and nobody who started after her got that answer. Her twenty years ended a few years into Carl's. The same few years of prices came at the end of her stretch, with all ten crates It's still lit, and at the start of his.

S29.asr: Same raise, same rule. Edna kept up, Ruth fell short late, and Carl fell far behind. In crates, Edna's row ended full. Ruth set about nine and Carl's at about four. What differed was the month each one started and what prices did after that.

S01.asr: Ruth's check rises every year and it buys less than her first one. At 65, she chose the smaller annuity check that rises 2 % a year and asked one thing. Would 2 % keep up with prices?

S02.asr: Her 20th year of checks ended this August. We tested that raise against every 20 -year stretch of U .S. prices since 1947 to see how often it kept its buying power and how much it usually kept.

S03.asr: Here, keeping up means a check still buys at least what its own first check bought. Ruth is an illustrative retiree, built on real U .S. prices. And today, her check falls short of that. This is U .S. only, and it's history, not a forecast. It doesn't say which check to choose.

S04.asr: At 65, an income annuity can pay a bigger check that never changes or a smaller check that rises by the same percentage every year. How much smaller the rising check starts depends on the insurer, and this video doesn't model it. So it can't compare the dollars both checks pay out over a lifetime. What it measures is buying power. What each check can buy, compared with what its own first check bought.

S05.asr: Ruth took her first rising check in August 2006. Her reasoning was simple, prices go up, and her check goes up too. So what does a raise of 2 % a year add up to?

S06.asr: After 20 raises, a check is 48 .6 % bigger than its first one. Over Ruth's 20 -year stretch, the consumer price index rose 64 .3%. That index is a national average of what urban households pay for, from rent to medical care to gasoline, not any one person's own basket.

S08.asr: Measured against its own first check, the bigger level check she turned down would buy about 6 in 10 today. So the raise slowed the loss. That's measured against each check's own start. And the level check started bigger by an amount this video doesn't model.

S09.asr: Year by year, Ruth Chek bought at least what her first one did on 12 of its first 15 anniversaries. It slipped under in a few early years, then climbed back each time.

S10.asr: In August 2021, at 80, her check still bought a little more than her first one did. Then in a single year, it fell below and it hasn't caught up since.

S11.asr: By August 2022, it bought 94 .5 % of what her first check did.

S12.asr: Measured against its own start, the level check she turned down fell that far much sooner. By year 5, it was already down to about 9 in 10. Her rising check stands there now, after 20 years. So was Ruth's stretch unusual? Or is this what a 2 % raise usually did?

S13.asr: We took every starting month from January 1947 to August 2006 and followed prices for 20 years after each one. That's 715 stretches, and Ruth's is one of them, the most recent. For each one, we asked Ruth's question. Did a check rising 2 % a year still buy at least what its first check bought? Each tile here is one stretch, lined up by the month it started.

S14.asr: it kept up in 17 of the 715. That's about 1 in 42.

S15.asr: Every one of those stretches started between September 1947 and January 1949. Since then, no starting month is kept up, including Ruth's.

S16.asr: In the typical stretch, prices rose 3 .1 % a year, so after 20 raises, the rising check typically bought 80 .7 % of what its first check bought. In crates, the typical rising check ended with most of its 10 still lit.

S17.asr: A level check over the same stretches typically kept 54 .3 percent, about half, and typically the level check had already sunk to where the rising check would end by about year eight. Again, that's buying power against each check's own start, not dollars paid.

S19.asr: Even the stretches that ran through the gentler 2000s and 2010s, the years closest to Ruth's own, fell short.

S21.asr: And over 25 years, not one stretch kept up.

S22.asr: We also ran it on the index Social Security uses for its yearly raises, with about the same result. On a gentler price measure, the raise kept up more often but still fell short in most stretches.

S23.asr: Then why did the same rays land so differently from one star to another?

S25.asr: After 20 raises, his check bought 43 .1 % of what his first check bought. A level check in his stretch would have bought 29%. His raise helped, and it still left him with less than half.

S26.asr: he wasn't alone. Stretches that began in the 1960s typically ended at 44 .3%.

S28.asr: and Ruth at 85 is still losing ground. In the year to this August, prices rose 3 .4%, more than her 2 % raise. That's one year of history, not a forecast for the year after it.

S30.asr: So what raise did keep up in this history? A raise of 3 % a year kept up in 42 .4 % of the 20 -year stretches. About 3 .1 % kept up in half. That's the typical rate from before, a median of the past, not an expectation. Keeping up in every stretch took the rate of Carl's years. These rates describe what prices did. This video doesn't say which check or which raise to choose.

S31.asr: The Consumer Price Index is a national average, not a retirees -owned basket, and health care and housing can weigh differently for someone Ruth's age. The 715 stretches overlap, so they're not 715 separate tests. And because annuity pricing isn't modeled, nothing here compares the dollars both checks pay out over lifetime. How we know this, and what's left out, is on this card and in the description.

S32.asr: This is U .S. only and it's history, not a forecast. 20 years ago, Ruth asked whether 2 % a year would keep up with prices. Her answer? For 15 years, mostly yes. And at 85, her check buys about nine crates for every 10 her first one bought.
